introduction: Construct an addition-polymer repeat, reconstruct its alkene monomer and preserve every original side group. Higher extensions build polyester repeats and distinguish actual condensation links from end-omitted notation.
scopeNote: Separate Chemistry: actual AQA8462 4.7.3.1–2 and limited Pearson9.17C–24C, paired2023 Foundation02/Higher08 questions and mark schemes, and actual RSC addition/condensation worksheets informed this original lesson. Addition transformations require no mechanisms or conditions. PVC/PTFE names are supplied for structural deduction. Condensation is clearly labelled Higher; acid-chloride examples are provided extensions with no acid-chloride recall required. Independent checks cover the shared/Foundation addition and structure-change demands; Higher construction/explanation tasks require independent self-review in practice. Earlier Polymer structures teaches physical structure/state; natural polymers and waste/material decisions have their later lessons. Every written/drawn response requires self-review, with no automatic examiner mark. Whole-course coverage and exam readiness remain unfinished.
outcomes: Represent alkene addition with single backbone bonds, original side groups, bracket continuations and lower-case n.
Deduce separate monomers from repeating units without losing or rearranging substituents.
Distinguish a monomer-derived repeat contribution, an equivalent phase, a crop and a complete molecule.
Conserve atom inventories and supplied relative-mass contributions without inventing end groups or addition by-products.
Distinguish covalent chemical changes from supplied intact-chain physical changes and use actual material evidence.
Higher: construct a diol/diacid-derived polyester repeat with both spacers, carbonyls and alcohol-derived linking oxygens.
Higher: explain functional-group requirements, small-molecule loss and context-specific finite-link versus idealised repeat counts.

warmup.title: Recognise the reacting group
warmup.prompt: Which supplied bond permits ordinary alkene addition polymerisation?

misconceptions.C–C only: A saturated alkane lacks the required alkene double bond.
misconceptions.C–H only: C–H is retained in the supplied alkene transformation.

warmup.explanation: The alkene C=C functional group reacts; the carbon skeleton and its side groups remain.

warmup.title: Recall carbon bonding
warmup.prompt: How many covalent bond orders does a neutral carbon normally have in these displayed structures?

misconceptions.Two: A double bond contributes two, but carbon needs four in total.
misconceptions.Five: Five exceeds the normal carbon valence in these examples.

warmup.explanation: Count a single bond as one and a double bond as two.
warmup.hint: Count bond orders rather than neighbouring atoms alone.

refresher.title: Small molecule to long chain
refresher.prompt: Which description distinguishes a monomer from its addition polymer?
refresher.answer: A small molecule joins with many others into a very large chain molecule
options: A small molecule joins with many others into a very large chain molecule
A monomer is an unchanged catalyst
The polymer must be a diamond-like network

misconceptions.A monomer is an unchanged catalyst: Its atoms become part of the polymer.
misconceptions.The polymer must be a diamond-like netwo: Ordinary addition polymer chains are large molecules, not automatically a three-dimensional covalent network.

refresher.explanation: Many separate monomer molecules become part of the same covalently bonded chain.

refresher.title: Find C=C
refresher.prompt: In chloroethene, which functional group enables addition polymerisation?

misconceptions.The chlorine alone: C–Cl remains; it is not the reacting alkene group.
misconceptions.The carbon–hydrogen bonds alone: Those bonds are retained in the repeating unit.

refresher.explanation: Circle the C=C group when recognising the polymerising alkene.
refresher.hint: Separate the reacting group from a substituent.

refresher.title: Change the reacting bond
refresher.prompt: What happens to C=C in the ordinary addition-polymer backbone?
refresher.answer: It becomes a C–C single bond
options: It becomes a C–C single bond
It stays C=C throughout the backbone

misconceptions.It stays C=C throughout the backbone: That would leave insufficient valence for the two outward chain connections.

refresher.explanation: Each former alkene carbon forms one new outward single bond to an adjacent unit.
refresher.hint: Keep four bond orders at each carbon.

refresher.title: Preserve substituents
refresher.prompt: When propene forms poly(propene), what happens to its CH3 group?
refresher.answer: It remains a side group on the same original reacting carbon
options: It remains a side group on the same original reacting carbon
Its carbon must become a third backbone carbon per unit

misconceptions.It leaves as methane: No small molecule is eliminated in addition polymerisation.
misconceptions.Its carbon must become a third backbone: The two reacting C=C carbons become the backbone pair.

refresher.explanation: The C3H6 inventory is retained; two C are in the backbone and one in the methyl substituent.
refresher.hint: Trace the atoms rather than changing the formula.

refresher.title: Keep carbon valence
refresher.prompt: After C=C becomes C–C, how many new outward chain bonds does EACH original alkene carbon form?

misconceptions.Two: Two extra outward bonds per carbon would exceed carbon valence.
misconceptions.None: The monomer-derived units must connect to neighbouring units.

refresher.explanation: One outward bond per carbon means two outward bonds for the two-carbon repeat altogether.
refresher.hint: Distinguish each carbon from each two-carbon unit.

refresher.title: Retain halogens
refresher.prompt: In the supplied tetrafluoroethene-to-PTFE transformation, what leaves as a small product?
refresher.answer: Nothing: all four F atoms remain in the repeat
options: Nothing: all four F atoms remain in the repeat

misconceptions.Four fluorine atoms: That loses atoms from the addition product.
misconceptions.Hydrogen fluoride: No H is present in this supplied monomer, and addition eliminates no small molecule.

refresher.explanation: A C2F4 repeat has the same atoms as the C2F4 monomer.
refresher.hint: Check both atom identity and reaction type.

refresher.title: Read a repeat
refresher.prompt: What do outward bonds passing through repeat brackets mean?
refresher.answer: The covalent chain continues beyond the shown unit
options: Extra H atoms must cap both ends
The unit is disconnected from its neighbours
The covalent chain continues beyond the shown unit

misconceptions.Extra H atoms must cap both ends: The brackets represent a repeating contribution, not a completed small alkane.
misconceptions.The unit is disconnected from its neighb: The continuation bonds mean the opposite.

refresher.explanation: Single bonds through both brackets connect repeated contributions.
refresher.hint: A crop is not a complete molecule.

refresher.title: Use repeat notation
refresher.prompt: Which notation convention is appropriate for an addition-polymer repeat?
refresher.answer: Lower-case n outside the brackets at the lower right
options: A number written as an extra atom
Lower-case n outside the brackets at the lower right

misconceptions.Upper-case N inside the unit: N is also the element symbol for nitrogen and is not the specified repeat-count convention.
misconceptions.A number written as an extra atom: The repeat count is notation, not another atom.

refresher.explanation: The brackets enclose the unit; n indicates many repetitions.
refresher.hint: Keep count notation separate from the atomic structure.

refresher.title: Recover a monomer
refresher.prompt: What change reconstructs a separate alkene from an addition-polymer-derived two-carbon repeat?
refresher.answer: Restore C=C and retain its original side groups
options: Keep both continuation bonds and n
Restore C=C and retain its original side groups

misconceptions.Delete halogens and add H: That changes the original atom inventory.
misconceptions.Keep both continuation bonds and n: Those belong to the polymer representation, not the separate monomer.

refresher.explanation: Remove polymer notation and continuation bonds; restore the alkene double bond.
refresher.hint: Trace the same pair of carbons in reverse.

refresher.title: Name poly(propene)
refresher.prompt: Which name follows from addition polymerisation of propene?

misconceptions.Poly(propane): The monomer was propene; changing the ending changes its identity.
misconceptions.Propane: This names a small alkane, not the polymer.

refresher.explanation: Use poly followed by the unchanged monomer name in parentheses.

refresher.title: Keep all atoms
refresher.prompt: Which comparison is true for an ordinary addition monomer and its monomer-derived repeat?
options: The repeat always gains two terminal H

misconceptions.The repeat always loses H2O: That is not ordinary addition polymerisation.
misconceptions.The repeat always gains two terminal H: Repeat ends indicate continuation, not capping atoms.

refresher.explanation: No other molecule is formed in addition polymerisation.
refresher.hint: Compare repeat contributions, not hypothetical chain end groups.

refresher.title: Multiply a repeat contribution
refresher.prompt: A supplied C2H4 repeat contribution has relative mass28. What is the contribution from three such units, ignoring omitted ends?
refresher.explanation: 3 × 28 = 84; this is a stated repeat contribution, not an exact whole-chain Mr.
refresher.hint: Multiply the supplied per-unit contribution by three.

refresher.title: Separate melting from polymerisation
refresher.prompt: In a supplied thermoplastic melting comparison, what changes without cutting its polymer backbone?
refresher.answer: Intermolecular attractions are overcome while chain covalent bonds remain
options: Intermolecular attractions are overcome while chain covalent bonds remain

misconceptions.Every chain bond must break: That describes a chemical change, not this intact-chain physical change.
misconceptions.No forces matter: Energy is needed to overcome attractions between the molecules.

refresher.explanation: Polymerisation forms covalent chain connections; this melting comparison separates intact molecules.

refresher.title: Higher: two reactive groups
refresher.prompt: Why can the supplied diol and diacid continue forming a polyester chain?
refresher.answer: Each molecule has two reactive functional groups
options: Any alcohol with one OH must form an indefinitely alternating chain
Each molecule has two reactive functional groups

misconceptions.Their names both contain carbon: Carbon alone does not provide the two functional groups.
misconceptions.Any alcohol with one OH must form an ind: A monofunctional reagent cannot continue the chain in both directions.

refresher.explanation: Two reactive ends permit repeated ester-link formation.

refresher.title: Higher: form one small molecule
refresher.prompt: In a supplied diacid/diol ester link, which fragments form water?
refresher.answer: Acid OH plus the H bonded to alcohol oxygen
options: The entire acid COOH plus the entire alcohol OH
Acid OH plus the H bonded to alcohol oxygen

misconceptions.The entire acid COOH plus the entire alc: That would remove the carbonyl carbon and linking oxygen.
misconceptions.Both carbonyl oxygens: Carbonyl O is retained in the polyester.

refresher.explanation: The alcohol oxygen remains in the ester link; the acid OH and alcohol H form H2O.

refresher.title: Higher: include the carboxyl carbons
refresher.prompt: HOOC–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH2–COOH has how many C atoms?
refresher.explanation: Four CH2 spacer carbons plus two carboxyl carbons give six.
refresher.hint: Each COOH also contains a carbon.

refresher.title: Higher: count a finite open chain
refresher.purpose: Higher: count a finite open chain
refresher.prompt: Five supplied monomer-derived nodes form ONE open, unbranched chain. Each connecting condensation link releases one water. How many waters form?
refresher.explanation: A five-node open chain has four actual links. End groups are retained in this finite model.

refresher.title: Higher: read the end-omitted repeat equation
refresher.purpose: Higher: read the end-omitted repeat equation
refresher.prompt: A standard idealised polyester repeat equation omits end groups and states two water losses PER repeat contribution. For n = 3 contributions, how many waters does THAT representation show?
refresher.explanation: The specified idealised representation shows 2n = 6 H2O. This is distinct from counting actual links in a finite open-chain diagram.
refresher.hint: Use the stated two-per-repeat convention; do not change its scope.

refresher.title: Link structure to different properties
refresher.prompt: Which statement explains why polymers can have different properties despite each having covalent chain bonds?
refresher.answer: Their chain structures and attractions between chains can differ
options: Their chain structures and attractions between chains can differ
Every polymer must have identical properties

misconceptions.Every polymer must have identical proper: Different monomers and chain arrangements can produce different behaviour.
misconceptions.No polymer has intermolecular attraction: Large separate chain molecules can interact with one another.

refresher.explanation: Covalent bonding within chains alone does not specify every bulk property. Use the actual chain structure and supplied material evidence.
refresher.hint: Distinguish the shared bond type from the full molecular structure.

guided.title: Build a repeat
guided.prompt: Build the ethene repeat. Which bond joins its two backbone carbons?

misconceptions.Double C=C: A retained double plus both outward bonds overfills carbon valence.
misconceptions.No bond: The two backbone carbons must remain covalently joined.

guided.explanation: Keep all four H; replace C=C by C–C and show chain continuation through both brackets.
guided.hint: Count bond orders at each carbon.

guided.title: Reconstruct the alkene
guided.prompt: After reversing the supplied chlorine-containing repeat, what distinguishes the separate monomer?
guided.answer: C=C with original side groups and no repeat notation
options: C=C with original side groups and no repeat notation
A chlorine-free molecule with two extra H

misconceptions.C–C with polymer brackets: That is still the polymer-derived representation.

guided.explanation: Restore the reacting double bond and retain three H and one Cl on their original carbons.

guided.title: Select one monomer-derived repeat
guided.prompt: In the supplied poly(propene) crop, how many TOTAL C atoms belong to one two-backbone-carbon monomer-derived repeat?
guided.explanation: Two backbone carbons plus one methyl side-group carbon give three.
guided.hint: Count side groups as well as the selected backbone.

guided.title: Audit five repeat contributions
guided.prompt: Five original ethene-derived contributions contain how many H atoms, ignoring omitted chain ends?
guided.explanation: 5 × 4 = 20 H atoms. No H2 or H2O is eliminated.

guided.title: Higher: explain repeated ester growth
guided.prompt: Use the original diacid/diol evidence. What permits continued alternating chain growth?
guided.answer: Two reactive groups on each supplied monomer
options: One reactive group on every molecule is enough
Two reactive groups on each supplied monomer

misconceptions.A gas bubble proves it: This structural requirement is not established by bubbles.

guided.explanation: Each ester link uses acid OH and alcohol H; the remaining reactive end can join another monomer.
guided.hint: Count functional groups on each original molecule.

guided.title: Higher: construct the actual repeat
guided.prompt: The supplied diol has two CH2 carbons and the diacid has two CH2 spacer carbons plus two COOH carbons. How many C atoms remain in one complete end-omitted repeat?
guided.explanation: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 C atoms; water loss removes no carbon.

guided.title: Higher: count actual links
guided.prompt: In the supplied six-node ONE open chain, each drawn condensation link releases one water. How many waters have formed?
guided.explanation: Six connected nodes have five actual links. This is the specified finite open diagram.

practice.title: Repair the retained double bond
practice.prompt: A proposed addition repeat retains C=C AND has outward single continuation bonds from both reacting carbons. What repair preserves the original atoms?
practice.answer: Change that C=C to C–C
options: Delete one H from each carbon

misconceptions.Delete one H from each carbon: That would change the original addition inventory.
misconceptions.Remove both continuation bonds permanent: That leaves a monomer rather than the requested linked repeat.

practice.explanation: One bond order is freed at each alkene carbon when C=C becomes C–C; each carbon forms one outward chain bond.
practice.hint: Audit local carbon valence.

practice.title: Reject a same-formula rearrangement
practice.prompt: The original repeat alternates CH2 and CCl2. A student draws CHCl and CHCl instead. Which judgement follows?
practice.answer: Wrong connectivity despite the same atom totals
options: Only the lower-case n is wrong
Wrong connectivity despite the same atom totals

misconceptions.Correct because C2H2Cl2 totals agree: The two original Cl were attached to one carbon, not one each.
misconceptions.Only the lower-case n is wrong: The substituent attachment pattern itself changed.

practice.explanation: Addition retains substituents on their original reacting carbons. Formula equality alone cannot verify this structure.
practice.hint: Trace which carbon each chlorine belongs to.

practice.title: Accept a reversed repeating unit
practice.prompt: The same propene-derived repeat is written –CH2–CH(CH3)– or –CH(CH3)–CH2– with correct brackets/continuations. Which judgement follows?
practice.answer: Equivalent reversed/shifted repeat representations
options: The second must lose its CH3
Only one direction is chemically valid

misconceptions.Only one direction is chemically valid: Orientation on the page does not define a different connectivity here.

practice.explanation: Either phase represents the same alternating two-carbon backbone pattern.
practice.hint: Follow the pattern beyond the brackets.

practice.title: Repair repeat-count notation
practice.prompt: A correct repeat has single continuation bonds through brackets but an uppercase N at the lower right. What is the specified repair?
practice.answer: Use lower-case n outside at the lower right
options: Use lower-case n outside at the lower right
Put lower-case n in place of a hydrogen

misconceptions.Change a carbon to nitrogen: N here was incorrect count notation, not an intended atom.
misconceptions.Put lower-case n in place of a hydrogen: The count must remain outside the structural unit.

practice.explanation: Use the conventional lower-case repeat count outside brackets.
practice.hint: Keep atoms separate from notation.

practice.title: Avoid inventing chain ends
practice.prompt: A repeat crop shows –CH2–CH2– with outward bonds through both brackets. Which interpretation is justified?
practice.answer: An end-omitted contribution continuing into a longer chain
options: An end-omitted contribution continuing into a longer chain
A complete C2H6 molecule with two added H

misconceptions.A complete C2H6 molecule with two added: The outward bonds are chain continuations, not end caps.

practice.explanation: The repeat inventory is C2H4; the complete polymer end groups are not specified.
practice.hint: Read the bonds through the brackets.

practice.title: Respect the stated representation
practice.prompt: A task explicitly asks for the unit derived from ONE supplied ethene monomer. Which backbone contribution meets that instruction?
practice.answer: Two carbons with four H
options: One CH2 group is always chemically impossible

misconceptions.One CH2 group is always chemically impos: A smaller CH2 translational motif can describe poly(ethene), but is not the stated one-monomer-derived representation.
misconceptions.Four carbons from two monomers: That is a larger repeated block, not the requested one-monomer contribution.

practice.explanation: The instruction requests C2H4 from one C2H4 monomer; distinguish representation scope from chemical impossibility.
practice.hint: Read what the stated unit represents.

practice.title: Name the addition product
practice.prompt: What is the ordinary addition-polymer name formed from propene?
practice.answer: Poly(propene)

misconceptions.Ethene: That is a different small alkene.

practice.explanation: Poly plus the unchanged monomer name gives poly(propene).
practice.hint: Retain the monomer ending.

practice.title: Count methyl-containing contributions
practice.prompt: Seven propene-derived C3H6 contributions contain how many C atoms, ignoring omitted chain ends?
practice.explanation: 7 × 3 = 21, including the methyl side-group carbons.
practice.hint: Count all carbons in each contribution.

practice.title: Avoid adding absent hydrogen
practice.prompt: Four supplied C2F4 repeat contributions contain how many H atoms?
practice.explanation: The supplied monomer contains no H; addition does not add it.
practice.hint: Read the actual original formula.

practice.title: Conserve chlorine atoms

practice.explanation: 5 × 1 = 5 Cl; no HCl is lost in this addition reaction.
practice.hint: Keep each original chlorine.

practice.title: Calculate a contribution
practice.prompt: A supplied ethene-derived contribution has relative mass28. What is the contribution from eight units, excluding omitted ends?
practice.explanation: 8 × 28 = 224. A precise full-chain Mr would require its actual end groups.
practice.hint: Multiply the supplied per-unit contribution.

practice.title: Conserve an addition feed

practice.explanation: Mass is conserved: all12.0g is incorporated under the explicitly stated conditions.
practice.hint: Use the stated complete conversion and absence of losses.

practice.title: Count units from the backbone
practice.prompt: An original crop contains18 BACKBONE carbons from a two-backbone-carbon alkene monomer. How many monomer-derived contributions are shown?
practice.explanation: 18 ÷ 2 = 9. Side-group carbons would not belong in this stated backbone count.
practice.hint: Use two backbone carbons per contribution.

practice.title: Distinguish atom and molecule counts
practice.prompt: A supplied idealised report joins200 separate alkene molecules into ONE chain, with no other product. Which counts are conserved?
